stem: A 17-year-old boy with epistaxis and nasal discharge undergoes a CT scan which shows unilateral low attenuation mass in the left maxillary sinus, with extension into the expanded nasal cavity and middle meatus. Some air remains in the affected sinus. A subsequent MRI shows the lesion to be bright on T2 with peripheral enhancement.
prompt: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
An inverted papilloma would demonstrate avid enhancement throughout as opposed to peripheral enhancement.

A mucocoele can be discounted due to the presence of some air remaining within the sinus.

An SCC in a 17-year-old would be unlikely and more associated with invasion than expansion of the spaces.

A juvenile angiofibroma should be considered in this demographic however the imaging features do not fit.

Antrochoanal polyps can widen the sinus ostia and cause smooth enlargement of the affected sinus.

stem: A 15-year-old boy suffers a knee injury while on a skiing holiday. He visits a local hospital and has x-rays taken of his knee. No fracture is found. Once back home he undergoes an MRI scan when the pain fails to resolve. There are tears to the anterior cruciate and medial collateral ligaments with bony contusions seen at the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
There is a lot of overlap between pivot shift injuries and clip injuries however the latter is not provided as an option.

Bony contusions

Bruising to the bone can be detected around 2 days following an injury but may not resolve for many months thereafter. With regards knee injuries, it is often possible to discern the mechanism of injury from the pattern of bruising seen. The contusions follow fluid on MRI scans i.e. low in signal on T1 and high on T2 (and STIR). STIR is used to suppress the fat of the bone marrow thereby making the fluid stand out more.

Clip injury and pivot shift injury

These two injuries are very similar. Both involve valgus stress on a flexed knee (such as a tackle to the knee during sports). A pivot shift injury also requires external rotation of the tibia. The three main structures most at risk during these injuries are:

Anterior cruciate ligament (especially in a pivot shift injury)

Medial collateral ligament (especially in a clip injury)

Medial meniscus (remember that the medial meniscus is attached to the medial collateral ligament

If all three are present together it is referred to as the O’Donoghue triad. Since O’Donoghue defined this triad however, it has been discovered that lateral meniscal tears are actually more common with this type of injury than medial meniscus ones.

Bony contusions occur at the side of impact because the proximal tibia and distal femur impact on one another thus:

Lateral tibial plateau (posterolateral in pivot shift injury)

Lateral femoral condyle

Transient lateral patella dislocation injury

When the patella dislocates laterally, its medial facet can impact onto the anterolateral corner of the lateral femoral condyle. Both areas become damaged and contusions can be seen on MRI. Often though, the patella reduces spontaneously and thus the exact mechanism of injury must be inferred from the imaging findings.

Joint effusion

Osteochondral injuries to the anterolateral femoral condyle and medial patella facet

Sprain or disruption to the medial retinaculum

Hyperextension injury

These occur often following excessively forceful kicking. There will be bony contusions at the anterior aspect of the tibial plateau and femoral condyles. Either of the anterior or posterior cruciate ligaments may also be involved.

Dashboard injury

As the name would suggest, this injury is usually stained by impact of the knee against the dashboard of a car during a road traffic incident. Force applied to the anterior aspect of the tibia when the knee is flexed leads to:

Osteochondral injury or fracture to the anterior aspect of the tibia

Posterior cruciate ligament rupture/sprain

stem: A 15-year-old boy with severe learning difficulties is brought to A+E by one of his full time carers who is concerned that he is now not himself, having last seen him two weeks previously. A thorough clerking and examination by a conscientious colleague of yours in A+E narrows the cause down to a possible testicular issue and you are asked to perform an ultrasound. Following appropriate consent procedures you find that the left testicle is enlarged and hypoechoic when compared to the right. You are unable to demonstrate any colour Doppler signal in either the testis or the epididymis. There is a small hydrocoele.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Testicular torsion

Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency with salvage rates dropping sharply beyond the first six hours. A normal ultrasound scan does not exclude testicular torsion, particularly if performed within the first six hours. Acute unilateral pain beginning at night is a typical history and the peak age range is in either newborn boys or young adolescents (13-16 years). Ultrasound features, if present, are as follows:

Hypoechoic compared to the normal side (after 6 hours)

Heterogenous if there is ischaemic necrosis present (after 24 hours)

Enlarged (after 8 hours)

Absent Doppler signal (incomplete torsion can show flow)

Twisting of the spermatic cord with spiralling vessels

Missed torsion

Where ultrasound features of heterogeneous testis with increased peri testicular flow but absent testicular flow are found in a patient with symptoms lasting longer than 24 hours, a missed torsion can be diagnosed.

Chronic torsion

Beyond around 10 days the testicle becomes small and homogeneously hypoechoic with an enlarged and echogenic epididymis.

Reversed torsion also known as torsion-detorsion sequence

Increased blood flow within the testicle is either caused by infection or reversed torsion (a testicular tumour can also show increased blood flow).

Epididymo-orchitis

Infection of the epididymis with concomitant infection of the testis is called epididymo-orchitis; it is seen most commonly in young adolescents with Chlamydia and Gonorrhoea accounting for most cases in this age range. In older patients E-coli and proteus are more likely to be responsible. Ultrasound is useful only in excluding testicular torsion as a cause of the pain (although a normal scrotal ultrasound does not exclude torsion), and investigating the possibility of abscess formation in cases refractory to antibiotic therapy. On ultrasound a reactive hydrocoele is often present and epididymal enlargement occurs. Colour Doppler flow can be used to demonstrate hyperaemia within the testicle and epididymis as would be expected for an infective process. Historically nuclear medicine scanning was used to confirm the diagnosis with findings of increased activity in the epididymis being expected owing to the hyperaemia.

stem: A skull radiograph is performed for assessment of asymmetric head in an otherwise well 2-year-old girl. On a Townes view there are two symmetrical 7mm well circumscribed lucencies seen posteriorly within the skull vault, one on either side of the child’s head. An ultrasound is requested which shows no overlying soft-tissue masses.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
There is a differential diagnosis for lytic lesions of the skull.

Parietal foramina

This is a benign congenital condition where the parietal bones fail to completely ossify leading to paired defects in the characteristic para-sagittal location. There are usually no clinical consequences.

Eosinophilic granuloma causes round punched-out type lesions, usually described as having a bevelled edge. These would usually be solitary although multiple lesions are definitely possible. The symmetry of the lesions described in the question goes against this on grounds of probability though.

Fibrous dysplasia can affect the skull. It is usually described as having a ground glass appearance with cortical expansion and a swell-defined sclerotic margin.

Osteogenesis imperfecta is not usually part of the differential diagnosis for lytic lesions in the skull. Multiple wormian bones are part of the diagnostic criteria and at a stretch leptomeningeal cysts caused by skull fractures due to fragility could be brought into the picture.

Sinus pericranii is largely a soft tissue (vascular) mass which can cause secondary effects on the skull, including a localised defect. Again though, bilateral symmetrical defects would be unusual.

stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to A+E following a fall from a trampoline. He is refusing to weight bear through his left leg and an x-ray reveals a fracture. The fracture line runs through the lateral aspect of the epiphyseal plate and the metaphysis.
prompt: What is the Salter-Harris classification of this fracture?
explanation:
***Please note that the vignette in this question states that the fracture runs through (ie along) the plate, not the epiphysis itself.***

Salter-Harris classification

Type I

S

Straight across the plate

5%

Type II

A

Above the plate

75%

Type III

L

Lower than the plate

10%

Type IV

T

Through both the epiphysis and the metaphysis

10%

Type V

ER

Erase the plate (crushed between the metaphysis and epiphysis

rare

The Salter-Harris classification is used to stratify fractures of the unfused skeleton according to their risk of developing deformity.

In the question the fracture is described as passing through the ‘lateral aspect of the epiphyseal plate and the metaphysis’. This denotes a Salter-Harris II. A Salter-Harris IV would go through the epiphysis, across the plate and through the metaphysis.

stem: A 3-year-old child with sickle cell disease is admitted with low-grade fever, irritability and crying on passive movement of the arm. There has been a history of diarrhoea for three weeks but no blood in the stools. Some basic blood tests are performed which show raised inflammatory markers. An abdominal ultrasound does not show any abnormalities but an MRI of the child’s elbow reveals bony oedema and a partly septated elbow effusion.
prompt: What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
explanation:
Although hopefully a septic arthritis would be being considered from the outset, and the patient should be receiving antibiotics even prior to their MRI scan, the damage done to a joint by a purulent effusion is best avoided by washing the joint out. This will have a faster therapeutic effect than antibiotic therapy and is therefore the priority in this case. The diagnosis of a septic joint is confirmed by aspiration of purulent joint fluid. Septations within the effusion are a strong indicator of septic arthritis.

Septic arthritis

Septic arthritis in any age group is a surgical emergency and the joint must be washed out as soon as feasible in order to avoid irreversible joint damage caused. Clinical suspicious must therefore be high, not least because early x-rays may be normal. Initial investigation should be with ultrasound and echogenic debris may be found within a joint effusion. The diagnosis is confirmed by aspiration of purulent joint fluid. The condition can also be readily appreciable on MRI which is very sensitive for early joint damage. Synovial oedema can be seen as high signal on T2 with enhancement post-gadolinium on T1 fat saturated sequences.

Age

Likely organism

Neonate

Group D strep

<4yrs

Haemophilus, Strep, staph aureus

>4yrs

Staph aureus

>10yrs

Staph aureus + Neisseria gonorrhoea

Adults

Staph aureus

stem: A 1-year-old girl is brought to A+E by her parents. She has severe abdominal tenderness and distension. Ultrasound demonstrates an ileocolic intussusception.
prompt: Which of the following is a contraindication to performing intussusception reduction?
options: Free abdominal gas on plain film
Intussusception length of greater than 3 cm
Lack of bowel vascularity on colour doppler
explanation:
Intussusception usually affects infants between the ages of 3 months and 3 years. The Ileocolic type is the most common, followed by ileo-ileocolic. It is important to consider lead points: HSP, Meckel’s diverticulum and duplication cysts are all possibilities.

Another important facet to this condition is the management of intussusception. Reduction using a fluoroscopic-guided air enema (rather than barium) reduces the risk of faecal peritonitis and is the preferred management. The risk of perforation with this method is thought to be around 0.5%. Free air on plain film and clinical peritonitis are contraindications to pneumatic reduction by air enema.

Although long intussusceptions, lack of bowel wall vascularity and an extended duration of symptoms are not favourable features (being associated with greater complication rates and poorer success rates of pneumatic reduction), they are not contra-indications; perforation is the only absolute contraindication here.

stem: A 3-month-old baby boy is brought in with progressive cyanosis and respiratory distress. His CXR shows a reduced number of lung markings in the periphery of a hyperinflated left upper lobe with flattening of the hemidiaphragms, and deviation of mediastinum to the right.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Congenital lobar overinflation (previously congenital lobar emphysema)

This condition is thought to be caused by underdevelopment of bronchial cartilage in the affected lobe(s). Consequently the bronchus is unable to remain patent during expiration leading to significant air trapping. It is usually the left upper lobe which is affected but approximately 40% of cases involve the left upper lobe; the right middle or the right upper lobes are affected in a further 55% of cases. There is a reasonable male preponderance of approximately 3:1.

On a CXR there is hyperlucency of the affected lobe and often mass effect on the mediastinum leading to contralateral mediastinal shift and thereby respiratory distress.

Pulmonary interstitial emphysema (PIE)

As the name would suggest, this disease is diagnosed when there is air within the interstitial tissues of the lungs. It is caused by alveolar rupture due to the barotrauma of mechanical ventilation or positive airway pressure. It can be associated with hyaline membrane disease and is prevalent in infants of a low birth weight. Complications such as pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum can be severe and acutely life threatening. Radiographically there is hyperinflation and lucencies in either a cystic pattern or streaks emanating from the hila and following the direction of the bronchi/bronchioles. It is treated with high frequency oscillation ventilation which is less traumatic to the lungs.

Swyer-James syndrome

In this condition, normal development of the infant lung is impeded by bronchiolitis (viral or mycoplasma) at an early age, with superadded acute airspace destruction. Consequently the affected lobe is small and lucent on the CXR due to air trapping. It is a differential diagnosis for a unilateral lucent hemithorax, along with a pneumothorax, very large pulmonary emboli and causes of decreased chest wall musculature such as Poland syndrome or, historically, polio. In an an exam situation Swyer-James syndrome is usually given as a teenage or young adult patient with a history of recurrent LRTIs. Air trapping, and bronchiectasis can also be described.

Congenital Pulmonary Airway Malformation (CPAM) – also known as Congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation (CCAM)

Although often an antenatal diagnosis, CPAM should be considered in the investigation of a neonatal respiratory distress. Milder cases can present later when the child develops a LRTI and decompensates. On investigation a cystic mass is discovered. The size of the cysts denotes the type with Type I accounting for half of cases and comprising a smaller number of larger (>20mm) cysts. Type III is more sponge-like with cysts measuring only a couple of mm and Type II is between the two. Where cysts are larger, air-fluid levels may be seen. The malformation can exert a mass effect, causing both hypoplasia of the remainder of the ipsilateral lung as well as contralateral mediastinal shift.

Tension pneumothorax

This must be ruled out for any patient presenting with acute respiratory distress. The presence of lung markings, even if scarce, ought to rule this out although the difference between ‘scarce’ and ‘absent’ is undoubtedly easier to interpret on a real CXR as opposed to a wooly description of one.

stem: A 3-day-old baby is referred for an ultrasound scan with ambiguous genitalia. The ultrasound demonstrates a normal uterus although the ovaries are not seen.
prompt: What is the most likely explanation? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)

Normal-appearing adrenal glands does not exclude a diagnosis of CAH however usually the classical appearance for the adrenal glands in a case of CAH is of diffuse enlargement with a so-called 'wrinkled' morphology. The word 'cerebriform' is often used to describe them and compares their appearance to that of the brain. The usual hypoechoic cortex and hyperechoic medulla is still seen but the enlarged gland is folded upon itself giving the wrinkled appearance. The role of ultrasound is also to discern any normal male or female anatomy. The normal uterus can usually be identified, if present, but the ovaries may simply be too small at birth to appreciate. In contrast, the normal testes, where present, should be visible with ultrasound from birth. Females usually present with ambiguous genitalia whereas males can present later with severe electrolyte imbalances.

Mullerian duct anomalies (MDA)

The two Mullerian ducts form separately then fuse in the first trimester to form all the structures between the upper vagina and the fallopian tubes. The final part of the amalgamation of the two sides is resorption of the central uterine septum.

Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome also known as EMG syndrome (Exomphalos, Macroglossia, Gigantism)

This curious condition crops up in a number of different radiology circles. It is caused by a mutation on chromosome 11 and leads to a specific set of clinical manifestations, chief among them are the three which give it the alternative name of EMG syndrome. Malrotation of the small intestine is another feature which has a high concordance with this condition.

stem: A 5-day-old baby boy is referred to the Emergency Department by the health visitor, who is concerned about his breathing. He is cyanosed and requires prompt intubation on arrival. A CXR is done and he is reviewed by the neonatal team who consider starting a prostaglandin infusion for a duct dependant lesion.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a duct dependent lesion? Select ONE answer only.
options: Infradiaphragmatic total anomalous pulmonary venous return
Transposition of the great arteries without a VSD
explanation:
Please note the question asks which answer is NOT a duct dependent lesion.

Duct dependant lesions are those where the patient deteriorates rapidly following the closure of the ductus arteriosus.

PDA - patent ductus arteriosus

A PDA accounts for around one in ten cases of congenital heart disease. In a normal patient the duct will close within hours of birth but in duct-dependant ciculations it may stay open for a few days before closing leading to an acute deterioration in the baby (classically around day 5 of life). Prostaglandins can be given to try to re-open the duct, or maintain what patency does exist at the time of presentation.

If the duct remains open in an otherwise normally formed heart the patient can develop heart failure due to the presence of a left to right shunt, but often patients are asymptomatic.

Duct dependent lesions:

Hypoplastic left heart syndrome

Severe coarctation

Interrupted arch

Pulmonary atresia

Severe Ebsteins anomaly

TGA (if no VSD)

Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR)

Anomalous pulmonary venous return can be partial or total. In the latter, the oxygenated blood returning from the lungs fails to drain into the left side of the heart but reaches the right side of the heart by other avenues. Such babies are dependent on a right-to-left shunt (usually an ASD). TAPVR is not a duct-dependant condition (which usually present around day 4-5 when the duct closes) but can also present in the very early neonatal period with unstable cyanosis.

Most patients with this condition return the oxygenated blood from the lungs to the right side of the heart via either the brachiocephalic veins or the coronary sinus. Excessive pressures on the lungs cause pulmonary plethora and, if not picked up antenatally or neonatally, can compensate for the initial few weeks and months. Owing to the prominence of the supracardiac vasculature, the appearance on a chest radiograph is said to resemble a snowman.

In the case of infradiaphragmatic TAPVR, the venous return from the lungs is via the portal vein or IVC. As the anomalous pulmonary vein passes through the diaphragm (at the oesophageal hiatus) it becomes compressed, leading to an acute presentation in the early neonatal period with pulmonary oedema. The heart size is usually normal and the patient may not have developed plethora by the time of presentation. Of importance to note, some patients with infradiaphragmatic TAPVR may benefit from prostaglandin therapy helping to maintain the ductus venosus in the abdomen. Depending on the exact anatomy of the anomalous venous drainage, the ductus venosus may be critical for circulation in a small number of these patients.

Congenital Cyanotic Heart Disease © Medical Exam Prep

stem: You are reviewing the chest radiograph of a 3-year-old girl. Her parents give a history of an acute choking episode which resolved quickly. They think she may have inhaled a peanut.
prompt: Which of the following is consistent with an inhaled foreign body? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Inhaled foreign body

This is an important differential diagnosis to consider in paediatrics, particularly in younger mobile children in whom an accurate history may not be forthcoming. Not all foreign bodies are radio-opaque. Inhaled foreign bodies are slightly more likely to enter the right main bronchus than the left owing to its straighter course but left sided foreign bodies are by no means unheard of. Usually an inhaled foreign body will cause a ball-valve mechanism on the affected side leading to air-trapping and overinflation. This gives rise to the CXR features described in the vignette. It is worth noting that the chest x-ray can also be normal in around a third of cases.

stem: A 3-day-old baby boy undergoes an ultrasound for obstructive urinary symptoms. There is bilateral hydronephrosis. You suspect he may have posterior urethral valves. He is investigated with a micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG).
prompt: Which of the following findings on the MCUG is consistent with this diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Reflux can be bilateral or unilateral. When unilateral it usually on the left side. The filling defect seen in the posterior urethra is curvilinear and orientated in a transverse manner.

The drooping lily sign is seen with suprarenal tumours such as a neuroblastoma.

The cobra head sign is seen with ureterocoeles.

The claw sign is seen in intrarenal masses such as Wilms tumours.

Poor corticomedullary differentiation is associated with posterior urethral valves however is not an MCUG finding, it is an ultrasound finding.

Posterior urethral valves

Posterior urethral valves is a condition restricted to baby boys and is sometimes diagnosed antenatally. The posterior urethra consists of the prostatic and membranous portions. The formation of valves here leads to outflow obstruction and dilatation of the posterior urethra. Obstruction causes the trabeculation of the bladder and reflux through the vesico-ureteric junction (which occurs more on the left than the right) causes hydronephrosis. The first line of investigation should be a micturating cystogram which will show fusiform dilatation of the posterior urethra and trabeculation of the bladder as well as any reflux. Prognosis is variable but some patients require renal replacement due to irreversible damage to the kidneys.

stem: A 12-year-old boy sustains a head injury with loss of consciousness and is found to have an extra-axial collection on CT.
prompt: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The classic presentation of an extradural haemorrhage is with an initial head injury causing transient loss of consciousness.

stem: A 3-year-old boy is reviewed in clinic. He has been diagnosed with heterotaxy, following closure of a large ASD closed shortly after birth.
prompt: Which of the following describes the most likely features of his condition? Select ONE answer only.
options: Bilobed lungs, polyplenia, normal liver position
Bilobed lungs, polysplenia, midline liver position
Trilobed lungs, asplenia, midline liver position
Trilobed lungs, asplenia, normal liver position
Trilobed lungs, polysplenia, normal liver position
explanation:
The patient most likely has polysplenia. It is uncommon for patients with asplenia to reach the age of 3 as almost all of them have TAPVR. ASD is a much more common finding with polysplenia.

Heterotaxy

There are two main forms of this congenital disorder:

Left sided isomerism (polysplenia)

Things that would usually be found on the left side are duplicated on the right side too. The most consistent features are the abnormalities of the spleen and IVC. The other features are commonly associated, but variably seen. The prognosis is slightly better than for asplenia syndrome as there is a lower association with congenital heart disease. There is still 75% mortality by age 5 though.

Spleen - multiple little spleens

IVC - interrupted IVC with azygos or hemiazygos continuation

Lung lobes - two on either side

Liver - situated centrally in the abdomen

Bowel - malrotation

Pancreas - truncated

Heart - ASD, VSD, PAPVR (less severe congenital heart disease)

Right sided isomerism (asplenia)

Things that would normally be found on the right side are duplicated on the left side too. Strong association with severe congenital heart disease means the condition has a mortality rate of 80% by age 1. Beyond that, the most consistent feature is the absence of the spleen. Once again, the other features are commonly associated, but variably demonstrated.

Heart - TAPVR and other anomalies (Almost 100% have severe cyanotic congenital heart disease)

Spleen - absent

Lung lobes - three on either side (specific finding)

Liver - normal position (can be midline or malpositioned)

Bowel - malrotation

IVC - on same side as aorta (usually the right)

Kidneys - associated with horseshoe kidney

stem: A 5-year-old girl who has suffered repeated chest infections undergoes a CT scan of her chest after an abnormality is detected on her CXR. There is a large soft tissue density mass within the left lower lobe. A blood vessel can be seen connecting the mass to the descending thoracic aorta. The mass seems to have its own pleural lining.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Swyer-James syndrome

In this condition, normal development of the infant lung is impeded by bronchiolitis (viral or mycoplasma) at an early age, with superadded acute airspace destruction. Consequently the affected lobe is small and lucent on the CXR due to air trapping. It is a differential diagnosis for a unilateral lucent hemithorax, along with a pneumothorax, very large pulmonary emboli and causes of decreased chest wall musculature such as Poland syndrome or, historically, polio. In an an exam situation Swyer-James syndrome is usually given as a teenage or young adult patient with a history of recurrent LRTIs. Air trapping, and bronchiectasis can also be described.

Bronchopulmonary foregut malformations:

CPAM

Sequestration

Duplication cysts (bronchogenic, neuroenteric, enteric)

Congenital Pulmonary Airway Malformation (CPAM) – also known as Congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation (CCAM)

Although often an antenatal diagnosis, CPAM should be considered in the investigation of a neonatal respiratory distress. Milder cases can present later when the child develops a LRTI and decompensates. On investigation a cystic mass is discovered. The size of the cysts denotes the type with Type I accounting for half of cases and comprising a smaller number of larger (>20mm) cysts. Type III is more sponge-like with cysts measuring only a couple of mm and Type II is between the two. Where cysts are larger, air-fluid levels may be seen. The malformation can exert a mass effect, causing both hypoplasia of the remainder of the ipsilateral lung as well as contralateral mediastinal shift.

Pulmonary sequestration

There are two types of pulmonary sequestration and two features which unite them. A segment of lung firstly, which derives its arterial blood supply from the systemic circulation and secondly, has no communication with the bronchial tree is termed pulmonary sequestration. It is a congenital abnormality and usually affects the left lower lobe with a smaller percentage affecting the right lower lobe.

Intralobar sequestration – This is more common (75%) but less severe. The affected segment does not have its own pleura and drains, like normal, via the pulmonary veins. Presents as recurrent pneumonias and is seen on a CXR as cysts with fluid levels. Some are associated with other congenital abnormalities but a larger proportion develop in isolation. A portion will contain air owing to communication via the pores of Kohn but they can also manifest as a soft tissue density mass.

Extralobar sequestration – This is less common (25%) and more severe with around half of patients suffering from other additional congenital anomalies. Venous drainage is via the systemic circulation, such as the IVC, and patients present in childhood either with respiratory distress due to shunting of blood or with symptoms attributed to the associated congenital anomalies (e.g. diaphragmatic hernia). The segment has its own pleura and therefore collateral air drift via the pores of Kohn cannot occur. The lack of aeration can help differentiate it from intralobar sequestration. Seen on a CXR as an opacity adjacent to the heart, abutting the diaphragm.

Image sourced from WikipediaCourtesy of RadsWiki CC BY-SA 3.0

Bronchogenic cysts

Unless particularly large, or infected, they are usually an incidental finding. Since they are a malformation of the bronchial tree they are lined with respiratory epithelium and hence fluid filled. They do not however communicate with the bronchial tree and therefore do not usually contain air. On CT they will be seen as a unilocular cyst with HU of water or slightly higher owing to the high protein content of water. Approximately half of cases are adjacent to the carina.

stem: A 14 -year-old girl confides in her mother that her periods have stopped. She denies being pregnant. Her GP requests an ultrasound and this shows a small ovarian lesion. Blood tests done concurrently show the βHCG is normal.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The top two answers for this question are a Leydig-Sertoli tumour and a Yolk sac tumour however only the former produces oestrogen and progesterone which would cause the amenorrhoea described in the vignette. Furthermore, although there is overlap, Leydig-Sertoli tumours tend to affect a slightly younger population than Yolk sac tumours. Yolk sac tumours are typically very aggressive, and usually very large at presentation. Presentation with a Yolk sac tumour is usually with a pelvic mass and associated symptoms.

Leydig-Sertoli tumour

Most patients with a Leydig-Sertoli tumour are in their early teens. Normal Leydig and Sertoli cells are found in the testes and produce testosterone and oestrogen respectively, among other hormones. Leydig-Sertoli tumours often produce one or both hormones in excess leading to virilisation and amenorrhoea, although some patients may experience no hormonal manifestations. AFP can be elevated though this is not usual. They are solid, fibrous tumours which can show cystic elements where haemorrhage or necrosis has taken place. Owing to their fibrous nature they usually return low signal on MRI, with/without high signal foci related to the cystic areas.

Granulosa cell tumours

These oestrogen producing tumours can affect women of any age. The excess oestrogen causes irregular or post menopausal bleeding. They tend to be large and multicystic with thick septations and a sponge-like appearance. Importantly they can be differentiated from epithelial ovarian tumours (e.g. Mucinous cystanedomas) by their lack of a feature described as intracystic papillary projections.

Corpus luteal cyst

The corpus luteum comprises the remnant of an ovarian follicle post ovulation. Without fertilisation the normal corpus luteum will involute spontaneously within 2 weeks but occasionally they can persist even in the absence of fertilisation and be seen as a corpus luteum cyst. Ultrasound characteristics depend slightly on the age of the cyst and the presence or absence of haemorrhage within it but a small (<3 cm) thick walled, rounded, cystic structure with peripheral vascularity (the so-called ‘ring of fire’) would be classical. A repeat ultrasound scan after 6 weeks (to ensure a different part of the menstrual cycle) is usually recommended.

Yolk sac tumour

These unpleasant germ cell tumours affect adolescents and can be quite large at presentation. A raised serum AFP is common. They are usually solid with or without cystic areas. Since they can arise from an ovarian dermoid sometimes fat signal can also be seen in association with these tumours.

Mature teratoma

Teratomas and dermoid cysts have very similar imaging characteristics despite their histological differences. Teratomas are the most common ovarian neoplasm but are slow growing and usually benign. By contrast immature teratomas are malignant. The presence of fat is a strong indicator for a mature teratoma with the combination of fat, fluid and calcification being highly specific. On MRI the fat will show the usual signal drop-out on gradient echo sequences. Calcification will show as low signal on T2. Although benign, mature teratomas can be complicated by torsion or rupture. Malignant degeneration if it does occur, is to squamous cell carcinoma most commonly.

stem: A 6-week-old girl is referred to the hospital by the health visitor for failure to progress. She undergoes an x-ray which shows cardiomegaly and a large mass in the right upper quadrant. An ultrasound scan reveals a complex poorly-defined 10cm mass in the right lobe of the liver which contains multiple vascular channels.
prompt: What pattern of calcification (if present) would be consistent with the diagnosis of a haemangioendothelioma? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Haemangioendothelioma

These are benign lesions which can cause elevation of the serum AFP and endothelial growth factor but the vast majority occur in babies under the age of 6 months. Around half of cases are associated with the presence of a cutaneous haemangioma. They are large vascular tumours and on imaging behave as might be expected of a giant haemangioma with heterogenicity on ultrasound, peripheral enhancement with gradual filling in on CT and flow voids on MRI. Calcifications can be seen with these lesions but they are finer, more granular calcifications; not coarse. Owing to their size they often cause significant right to left shunting of blood resulting in congestive heart failure. Thrombocytopaenia also occurs due to platelet trapping (known as the Kasabach-Merritt sequence). N.B. these lesions should not be confused with epithelioid haemangioendotheliomas which occur in adults.

stem: An 11-year-old previously healthy girl presents to a minor injuries unit with a 4 day history of headache, lethargy, malaise and sinus congestion. She suffers a seizure whilst being transferred from the minor injuries unit to the local paediatric centre. She undergoes a CT head scan which shows among other things a soft tissue density lesion overlying the supraorbital region of the frontal bone.
prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
explanation:
Pott puffy tumour

During an acute sinusitis there is bony erosion and subperiosteal abscess formation. Extracranially this causes forehead swelling, hence the name of this entity. Additionally there can also be the usual intracranial extension as a complication of frontal sinusitis, hence the presentation with seizures.

stem: You are performing an ultrasound scan on a 4-year-old boy whose parents are concerned that his stomach has become very large. There is a large mass in the left retroperitoneal space. It is heterogeneous in echotexture. The boy goes onto have a CT scan which shows displacement of the IVC and curvilinear calcification. You suspect he may have a Wilms tumour.
prompt: Which of the following syndromes does not predispose to Wilms tumour? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome is a very rare condition which predisposes to chromophobic RCCs. Patients also suffer from pulmonary cysts (increased risk of spontaneous pneumothorax) and fibrofolliculomas (benign fibrous tumours related to the hair follicles).

Predisposing syndromes for Wilms tumour

Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome - macroglossia, hemihypertrophy, visceromegaly, omphalocoele

DRASH syndrome - progressive glomerulonephritis and male pseudohermaphroditism

WAGR syndrome - Wilms tumour, aniridia, GU abnormalities, mental retardation

Perlman syndrome - polyhydramnios, macrocephaly, visceromegaly

Golabi-Behmel syndrome - macrostomia, macroglossia, occular hypertelorism

Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma)

This is the most common abdominal mass in children under the age of 8. There are reasonably strong associations with renal anomalies, genital anomalies, aniridia and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (although the last of these also has an association with neuroblastoma). Presentation is usually with an abdominal mass and/or pain.

On imaging the masses are usually heterogenous. Cystic areas can often be seen secondary to areas of necrosis. The claw sign occurs when there is a rim of normal renal tissue extending part of the way around the mass. A Wilms tumour is often described as enhancing but less so than the adjacent normal renal parenchyma.

Renal cell carcinoma

After around the age of 11 the incidence of Wilms tumours and renal cell carcinomas are approximately equal. It can be extremely difficult, nigh on impossible, to tell the two apart on imaging characteristics alone. In general however, renal cell carcinomas are more likely to present with haematuria whereas Wilms tumours, being usually very large, are more likely to present as a large abdominal mass. Both can exhibit calcification, though this is more common in renal cell cancer, and both can invade the renal veins or IVC. Any child diagnosed with a renal cell carcinoma must be screened for von Hippel Lindau syndrome.

stem: A 9-day-old baby boy who was born prematurely is found to have bubbly and curvilinear areas in the right lower quadrant on abdominal x-ray.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Of the neonatal causes of bowel obstruction, the age at presentation and level of obstruction can point heavily towards the diagnosis.

Level of obstruction

Age at presentation

NEC

All/any

<10 days

Meconium ileus

Caecum/terminal ileum

<48hrs

Meconium plug

Splenic flexure

<48hrs

Hirschsprung disease

Sigmoid colon

<6 weeks

Necrotising enterocolitis

This is the most common gastrointestinal emergency for premature babies. It results from an immature immune system being unable to cope with mucosal ulceration. Almost all cases occur before the baby reaches 10 days old. Pneumatosis intestinalis (intramural gas) is the hallmark of the condition on abdominal radiography and appears as curvilinear or bubbly areas. Branching gas within the liver, indicative of portal venous gas can also occur but is not as serious a finding as it would be for an adult. Surgery is definitely indicated however, if there is evidence of perforation and for this reason patients should undergo a horizontal beam x-ray. If performed decubitus the left side should be down in order to better visualise air against the contour of the liver. On an over-table view the ‘football’ sign, where a large collection of gas rises centrally, is seen if there is sufficient free gas within the abdomen.

Meconium ileus

This condition is strongly associated with cystic fibrosis but not with prematurity. The thicker-than-normal intestinal mucus, increase in transit time and pancreatic insufficiency all conspire to cause impaction of meconium leading to small bowel obstruction in neonates. It should be suspected if the baby does not pass meconium within the first 2 days of life. On an abdominal radiograph there will be no air-fluid levels since no fluid is present but multiple gas filled dilated loops of small bowel will be seen. The meconium can sometimes be seen as a bubbly area in the right lower quadrant where it has impacted within the terminal ileum.

Meconium plug

Whereas meconium ileus leads to small bowl obstruction, meconium plug syndrome leads to large bowel obstruction due to functional immaturity of the colon. This will also present within the first two days of life with a failure to pass meconium. Some literature associates this condition with babies born to diabetic mothers and around a quater of patients have cystic fibrosis. The condition can be treated with a water-soluble contrast enema.

Meconium peritonitis

When there is antenatal bowel perforation the result is a chemical peritonitis as opposed to a purulent one since the bowel is as yet unpopulated by the usual flora of life after birth. The result is calcification scattered around the abdomen. If the perforation spontaneously heals itself then the prognosis is excellent and the finding of abdominal calcification may be purely incidental.

Hirschsprung disease

There is a congenital absence of parasympathetic ganglia in the muscular and submucosal layers of a segment of colon, usually the sigmoid colon. The affected segment is unable to relax to pass meconium and patients therefore present with failure to pass meconium or sometimes within the first six weeks of life with severe constipation with overflow diarrhoea. Classically on a barium enema there is an inverted cone shape formed between the normal and abnormal bowel segments and the diagnosis should be confirmed using a suction biopsy below this transition point. Another feature seen on a barium enema is a result of abnormally coordinated contractions of the affected segment which appears as so-called ‘persistent corrugation’.

stem: A fair-haired 6-year-old boy undergoes a CT chest for further investigation of recurrent chest infections. This demonstrates lower lobe predominant bronchiectasis. The heart is in the expected position.
prompt: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia

This predominantly causes bronchiectasis in the middle and lower lobes. Only 50% have Kartagener’s syndrome (A triad of situs inversus, sinusitis and bronchiectasis), hence the normal heart position in the question. Affected men are infertile, and women are subfertile.

ABPA

This is generally only seen in asthmatics and is characterised by central bronchiectasis particularly in the mid-zones and sometimes upper zones. Centrilobular nodules are also a feature.

Aspiration

This classically causes lower lobar bronchiectasis, but not in this demographic without mention of risk factors for aspiration in the history.

Cystic Fibrosis

This is causes bronchiectasis but predominantly affects the upper lobes. Don’t be fooled by the mention of fair hair which is a red-herring in this question.

Middle Lobe Syndrome

This affects the middle lobe or lingula. Chronic atelectasis arises secondary to airway obstruction from any one of a multitude of different causes (some benign, some malignant) and associated bronchiectasis can develop. Other areas are not usually affected.

stem: A 6-year-old girl is taken by her parents to the GP after they noticed her abdomen was getting bigger. On examination there is a right upper quadrant mass. The GP refers the girl to the local hospital where blood tests reveal an elevated serum AFP level. She undergoes an MRI scan and the mass returns high signal on T2 although there are some low intensity bands running through it. You th ink the patient may have a hepatoblastoma.
prompt: What pattern of calcification (if present) would be consistent with the diagnosis of a hepatoblastoma? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Hepatoblastoma

This is the most common primary liver tumour in infants under the age of 5. It is associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann Syndrome and prematurity. Most hepatoblastomas are found in children under the age of 3 but they can occur at any point in childhood. They are the third most common abdominal tumour in children. Presentation is typically with an abdominal mass and weight loss and the serum AFP is often markedly elevated. Some may produce hormones and thereby precocious puberty but this is rare. Coarse calcification is seen in around a third of cases. On ultrasound the mass will be large and heterogenous. On CT they appear as a predominantly low attenuation mass seeming to consist of multiple confluent nodules. Often the rim of the mass enhances well on CT. On MRI they are, for the most part, high in signal on T2 weighted sequences but can show low intensity fibrous bands running through them.

Hepatic masses in children © Medical Exam Prep

stem: A 5-day-old baby boy is referred to the Emergency Department by the health visitor, who is concerned about his breathing. He is cyanosed and requires prompt intubation on arrival. A radiograph shows a normal heart size but bilateral air-space opacities. The pulmonary vasculature appears normal.
prompt: Which of the following cardiac conditions is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
The heart size may be normal and the patient may not have yet developed pulmonary plethora in the case of infradiafragmatic TAPVR.

-----------------------

Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR)

Anomalous pulmonary venous return can be partial or total. In the latter, the oxygenated blood returning from the lungs fails to drain into the left side of the heart but reaches the right side of the heart by other avenues. Such babies are dependent on a right-to-left shunt (usually an ASD). TAPVR is not a duct-dependant condition (which usually present around day 4-5 when the duct closes) but can also present in the very early neonatal period with unstable cyanosis.

Most patients with this condition return the oxygenated blood from the lungs to the right side of the heart via either the brachiocephalic veins or the coronary sinus. Excessive pressures on the lungs cause pulmonary plethora and, if not picked up antenatally or neonatally, can compensate for the initial few weeks and months. Owing to the prominence of the supracardiac vasculature, the appearance on a chest radiograph is said to resemble a snowman.

In the case of infradiaphragmatic TAPVR, the venous return from the lungs is via the portal vein or IVC. As the anomalous pulmonary vein passes through the diaphragm (at the oesophageal hiatus) it becomes compressed, leading to an acute presentation in the early neonatal period with pulmonary oedema. The heart size is usually normal and the patient may not have developed plethora by the time of presentation. Of importance to note, some patients with infradiaphragmatic TAPVR may benefit from prostaglandin therapy helping to maintain the ductus venosus in the abdomen. Depending on the exact anatomy of the anomalous venous drainage, the ductus venosus may be critical for circulation in a small number of these patients.

Congenital Cyanotic Heart Disease © Medical Exam Prep

stem: A 4-month-old baby is reviewed in the paediatric clinic following concerns regarding his head.
prompt: A flat, widened skull shape with ‘harlequin eye’ and premature closure of the coronal sutures describes which of the following craniosynostosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation: The most common suture to undergo premature closure is the Sagittal suture which gives Dolichocephaly/ scaphcephaly (long and skinny). Closure of the metopic suture gives a pointed forehead known as Trigonocephaly. Coronal suture closure is known as brachycephaly which also gives a ‘harlequin eye’ appearance, so called because it causes elevation of the superior orbital margins giving the baby a quizzical expression. It can occur unilaterally  in cases of plagiocephaly. Bilateral (turricephaly) lambdoid premature suture closure have also been described.

stem: With regards a fracture to the base of the 5th metatarsal, which of the following would be the most common findings?
prompt: Select one answer only.
options: Fracture line at 90o to the diaphysis, stable, associated avulsion of peroneus brevis
Fracture line at 90o to the diaphysis, stable, associated avulsion of peroneus longus
Fracture line at 90o to the diaphysis, unstable, associated avulsion of peroneus longus
Fracture line lateral to the diaphysis, stable, associated avulsion of peroneus brevis
Fracture line lateral to the diaphysis, unstable, associated avulsion of peroneus longus
explanation:
The apophysis of the fifth metatarsal is laterally placed with respect to the diaphysis. It appears around the age of 11 and fuses within around 3 years.

Fractures of the base of the fifth metatarsal typically occur at 90o to the diaphysis.

Peroneus brevis inserts onto the lateral aspect of the base of the fifth metatarsal.

Peroneus longus follows a similar course to peroneus brevis initially but then crosses the plantar surface of the metatarsal heads and inserts into the base of the first metatarsal.

stem: You are reviewing the chest radiograph of a 3-year-old girl. There is increased intrathoracic volume in the left chest with flattening of the hemidiaphragm.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT consistent with an inhaled foreign body? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which feature is NOT consistent with an inhaled foreign body.

Inhaled foreign body

This is an important differential diagnosis to consider in paediatrics, particularly in younger mobile children in whom an accurate history may not be forthcoming. Not all foreign bodies are radio-opaque. Inhaled foreign bodies are slightly more likely to enter the right main bronchus than the left owing to its straighter course but left sided foreign bodies are by no means unheard of. Usually an inhaled foreign body will cause a ball-valve mechanism on the affected side leading to air-trapping and over-inflation. This gives rise to the CXR features described in the vignette. It is worth noting that the chest x-ray can also be normal in around a third of cases.

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the Emergency Department by his parents. They report that he fell over the back of their sofa and hit his head. He is examined and x-rays are taken.
prompt: Which of the following is suggestive of an accidental injury? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
**Please note the question asks for the answer most likely to be caused by an ACCIDENTAL injury**

Spiral fractures can be caused by both accidental and non-accidental injuries but are more common in adults than children. Significant power is needed to cause a spiral fracture in a child; they are unusual in the setting of a straightforward fall.

Non-accidental injury

It is the responsibility of all members of the healthcare profession to be alert to the possibility of non-accidental injury. For radiologists, there are specific findings which should alert the reporter to the possibility of non-accidental injury. These include:

Lower limb injuries in a non-ambulant child

Discrepancy between the history and apparent injuries

Delay seeking medical attention

Metaphyseal fractures (corner or bucket-handle)

Multiple fractures of different ages

Scapula fractures

Posterior rib fractures

Sternal fractures

Skull fractures (especially non-parietal, or crossing sutures)

It is important to appreciate that any fracture (not just the ones listed above) can be caused by non-accidental injury.

A skeletal survey to investigate for the presence of further fractures includes:

Two views of the skull (frontal and lateral)

AP of upper limbs (over multiple films if necessary)

DP of wrist/hand

Lateral of elbow and wrist

AP of lower limbs (over multiple films if necessary)

DP feet

AP ankle

Lateral of ankle and knee

AP abdomen and pelvis

Three views of the chest (frontal and two oblique)

Lateral whole spine

CT head - if younger than 1 year, or older than 1 year with head trauma or abnormal neurology, or older than 2

Siblings younger than age 2 should also have the same imaging as the index patient.

stem: A 12-year-old girl who has been complaining of abdominal pain for the last three months is referred to the local hospital by her GP for investigation. On examination she has a mass in her right upper quadrant and an ultrasound scan shows a solitary echogenic mass. It is well defined but has a hypoechoic central scar. On a CT scan there is arterial enhancement and washout on the portal venous phases. The scar does not enhance but calcification can be seen within it.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Paediatric liver lesions with a raised AFP

Lesion

Usual age

Features

Infantile haemangioendothelioma

<6m (NB AFP can be normally elevated in this age range)

Heart failure, low platelets. Vascular lesion, fine granular calcifications.

Hepatoblastoma

6m-3y

Coarse calcification, rim enhancement.

HCC

>5y

Central scar which can calcify

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) also known as Hepatoma

There is a peak in the incidence of HCCs in the paediatric age range at around age 13. The central scar of an HCC is a specific feature which can help separate it from potential differential diagnoses. Although calcification of this central scar is seen in around a quarter of cases there tends to be less calcification in HCCs than there would be in a hepatoblastoma.

Although metastases are the most common cause of malignant hepatic lesions, hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary hepatic malignancy. It usually arises on a background of cirrhosis of any cause. Patients with any of the hepatitis viruses, alcoholic cirrhosis, haemochromatosis, and Wilson disease are all at risk. Carcinogens such as thorotrast and aflatoxin also predispose to HCC formation. Serum alpha fetoprotein levels are often raised, in contrast with cholangiocarcinomas which are one of the main differential diagnoses.

On imaging HCCs can have a variety of appearances. A large irregular mass with satellite nodules is the most common finding but a diffuse infiltrative version can also occur. Since HCCs derive their blood supply from the hepatic artery they show arterial enhancement on CT with washout on later phases. On ultrasound HCCs tend to be hyperechoic when compared to the rest of the liver and on MRI they show variable signal intensity on both T1 and T2 but arterial enhancement with venous washout can again be seen once Gadolinium has been given.

Infantile haemangioendothelioma

These are benign lesions which can cause elevation of the serum AFP but the vast majority occur in babies under the age of 6 months. Around half of cases are associated with the presence of a cutaneous haemangioma. They are large vascular tumours and on imaging behave as might be expected of a haemangioma showing peripheral enhancement with gradual filling in on CT and flow voids on MRI. Calcifications can be seen with these lesions but they are finer, more granular calcifications; not coarse. Owing to their size they often cause significant right to left shunting of blood resulting in congestive heart failure. Thrombocytopaenia due to platelet trapping (known as the Kasabach-Merritt sequence). N.B. these lesions should not be confused with epithelioid haemangioendotheliomas which occur in adults.

Hepatoblastoma

Most hepatoblastomas are found in children under the age of 3 but they can occur at any point in childhood. They are the third most common abdominal tumour in children. Presentation is typically with an abdominal mass and weight loss and the serum AFP is often markedly elevated. Some may produce hormones and thereby precocious puberty but this is rare. Coarse calcification is seen in around a third of cases. On ultrasound the mass will be large and heterogenous. On CT they appear as a predominantly low attenuation mass seeming to consist of multiple confluent nodules. Often the rim of the mass enhances well on CT. On MRI they are, for the most part, high in signal on T2 weighted sequences but can show low intensity fibrous bands running through them.

Wilms tumour also known as a nephroblastoma

This is the most common abdominal mass in children under the age of 8. There are reasonably strong associations with renal anomalies, genital anomalies, aniridia and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (although the last of these also has an association with neuroblastoma). Presentation is usually with an abdominal mass and/or pain.

10% tumour – Wilms

Calcification

Vascular invasion

Bilateral

Lung metastases

Poor histology

On imaging the masses are usually heterogenous. Cystic areas can often be seen secondary to areas of necrosis. The claw sign occurs when there is a rim of normal renal tissue extending part of the way around the mass. A Wilms tumour is often described as enhancing but less so than the adjacent normal renal parenchyma.

Hepatic abscess

Liver abscesses can occur in children, for much the same reasons as they arise in adults, although they are far more common in adults. Pyogenic abscesses result from bacteria accessing the liver via the biliary tree, septicaemia, direct spread, trauma or during a liver procedure. Patients are usually in their 60s. Amoebic abscesses occur in slightly younger patients (40s) and tend to result from spread of amoebae from the colon via the portal venous system. On ultrasound they appear as a hypoechoic mass with posterior acoustic enhancement. Internal debris may be apparent. On CT they are usually low in attenuation with rim enhancement. MRI signal characteristics are dependent on the protein content of the pus but usually abscesses return little T1 signal and, owing to their fluid nature, return high signal on T2 weighted sequences.

It is said that amoebic abscesses are usually found to be contiguous with the liver capsule.

stem: A 12-year-old boy undergoes a contrast enhanced CT chest for further investigation of an anterior mediastinal mass which was found on a chest radiograph. The mass is large with a lobulated outline, but with no invasion of adjacent structures. There are enlarged lymph nodes in the included cervical chains. There is no calcification, fat or haemorrhage within the mass.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Lymphoma

This is the most common anterior mediastinal mass in children. It may be difficult to differentiate a lymphoma from normal thymus, particularly in a patient younger than 10 years of age. Associated lymphadenopathy (i.e. cervical) can be the key to distinguishing the two pathologies. Calcification is rare prior to any treatment but can be a feature of lymphoma which has been treated.

Germ Cell Tumour

This often causes a large anterior mediastinal mass. It can be subdivided into Teratoma (usually cystic with fat and calcification), seminoma (bulky and lobulated) and Non-seminomatous Germ Cell Tumour (haemorrhage and necrosis).

Duplication cyst

These are very rarely found in the anterior mediastinum, usually being posterior mediastinal (neuroenteric) or middle mediastinal (bronchogenic, enteric).

Askin Tumour

These heterogenous tumours are part of the Ewing Sarcoma spectrum. Patients are often in their early teens. Askin tumours displace rather than invade adjacent mediastinal structures although rib destruction is common and is a fact which can help distinguish it from a pleuropulmonary blastoma which is another cause of a large mediastinal mass, albeit usually found in babies under the age of 2, but which does not cause rib destruction.

stem: A 1-year-old girl is brought to A&E by her parents. She has severe abdominal tenderness and distension. Ultrasound demonstrates an ileocolic intussusception. The paediatric consultant phones you to arrange a fluoroscopic intussusception reduction.
prompt: Which of the following is NOT a contraindication to performing intussusception reduction? Select ONE answer only.
options: Free abdominal gas on plain film
Lack of bowel vascularity on colour doppler
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is NOT a contraindication.

Intussusception usually affects infants between the ages of 3 months and 3 years. The Ileocolic type is the most common, followed by ileo-ileocolic. It is important to consider lead points: HSP, Meckel’s diverticulum and duplication cysts are all possibilities. Another important facet to this condition is the management of intussusception. Reduction using a fluoroscopic-guided air/CO2 enema (rather than barium) reduces the risk of faecal peritonitis and is the preferred management. The risk of perforation with this method is thought to be around 0.5%. Free air on plain film and clinical peritonitis are contraindications to pneumatic reduction by air enema.

Although long intussusceptions, lack of bowel wall vascularity and an extended duration of symptoms are not favourable features, perforation is the only absolute contraindication here.

Intussusception reduction

Reduction should be performed only in a hospital equipped to deal with any complications which may arise; this usually means it is only performed in centres where there are on-site paediatric surgical services. Parental understanding and consent are obviously of paramount importance too. Reduction using a fluoroscopic-guided air enema (rather than barium) reduces the risk of faecal peritonitis and is the preferred management. The risk of perforation with this method is thought to be around 0.5%. Free air on plain film and clinical peritonitis are contraindications to pneumatic reduction by air enema.

Ensure adequate staffing support present and working IV cannula in situ

Take a cross table or lateral decubitus film to exclude free gas

Lie patient supine

Insert catheter into the rectum as far as possible without significant pressure

Insufflate slowly to 60-100mmHg with carbon dioxide while screening to identify intussusceptum

Screen intermittently for 3 minutes with the aim of observing the intussusceptum retreating back to the iliocaecal valve, and/or air entering the terminal ileum.

After 3 minutes release the pressure and wait for a couple of minutes

Repeat a further 2 times (three in total) if necessary

If successful, obtain a cross table film to exclude free gas

stem: An 18-month-old boy undergoes a CT chest for further investigation of a mass identified on chest radiograph following a presentation with general malaise, shortness of breath and absent air entry in the right hemithorax. The CT demonstrates a large, heterogeneous, enhancing mass which fills the entire right hemithorax and is displacing the mediastinum to the left. No rib destruction is seen, despite the mass pressing against the chest wall.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
An extremely large hemithoracic mass in a 1-2-year-old child is almost always either an Askin tumour or Pleuropulmonary blastoma. Rib or bony involvement is the key differentiation feature. Pleuropulmonary blastoma does not cause rib destruction, whereas an Askin tumour would.

Pleuropulmonary blastoma

This is a primary intrathoracic malignancy. It can resemble a Congenital Cystic Adenoid Malformation. They generally do not contain calcification and 'never' invade the skeleton. There is an association with multilocular cystic nephroma in around 10% of cases.

Askin Tumour

These heterogenous tumours are part of the Ewing Sarcoma spectrum. Patients are often in their early teens. Askin tumours displace rather than invade adjacent mediastinal structures. Rib destruction is common and is a fact which can help distinguish it from a pleuropulmonary blastoma which is another cause of a large mediastinal mass, albeit usually found in children under the age of 2, but which does not cause rib destruction.

Neuroblastoma

For a posterior mediastinal mass in a child under the age of 10, a neuroblastoma should be the top differential diagnosis to be considered. Usually it is heterogeneous with calcification and areas of necrosis.

Lymphoma

This is the most common anterior mediastinal mass in children. It may be difficult to differentiate a lymphoma from normal thymus, particularly in a patient younger than 10 years of age. Associated lymphadenopathy (i.e. cervical) can be the key to distinguishing the two pathologies. Calcification is rare prior to any treatment but can be a feature of lymphoma which has been treated.

stem: A 16-year-old boy who is otherwise fit and well has a CXR for insurance purposes which shows a bump at the left hemidiaphragm. There is a lateral view which shows a soft tissue opacity posteriorly with discrete upper margins.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bochdalek hernia

A congenital defect in the posterior aspect of the diaphragm which usually (80%) occurs on the left and accounts for around 90% of all diaphragmatic hernias. They tend to be Big, at the Back (ie posterior), present as a Baby, contain Bowel, and can be quite Bad since they are associated with pulmonary hypoplasia due to mass effect. They can however, be small and asymptomatic. The exact content of the hernia will depend on the laterality. In real life radiology when they occur on the right they may be as an occult finding of a right lower zone mass silhouetted against the diaphragm. Despite the classical appearance on a CXR, a CT is usually performed for confirmation.

Morgagni hernia

A congenital defect in the anteromedial aspect of the diaphragm. At approximately 5% of all diaphragmatic hernias, Morgagni hernias are much less common than Bochdalek hernias which account for a further 90%. It is usually just omental fat which is found within the hernia but abdominal viscera can also herniated. (Conversely a Bochdalek hernia usually contains viscera but can contain just fat). Morgagni hernias tend to be small and asymptomatic, hence they usually present as incidental findings. The closest differential diagnosis to a Morgagni hernia would be a cardiac fat pad. Given coronal or sagittal CT slices it should be easy to see the omental vessels coursing upwards from the abdomen through the diaphragmatic defect. There will be vessels supplying a cardiac fat pad but these are likely to be far smaller.

Pulmonary sequestration

There are two types of pulmonary sequestration and two features which unite them. A segment of lung firstly, which derives its arterial blood supply from the systemic circulation and secondly, has no communication with the bronchial tree is termed pulmonary sequestration. It is a congenital abnormality and usually affects the left lower lobe with a smaller percentage affecting the right lower lobe.

Intralobar sequestration – This is more common (75%) but less severe. The affected segment does not have its own pleura and drains, like normal, via the pulmonary veins. Presents as recurrent pneumonias and is seen on a CXR as cysts with fluid levels. Some are associated with other congenital abnormalities but a larger proportion develop in isolation.

Extralobar sequestration – This is less common (25%) and more severe with around half of patients suffering from other additional congenital anomalies. Venous drainage is via the systemic circulation and patients present in childhood either with respiratory distress due to shunting of blood or with symptoms attributed to the associated congenital anomalies (e.g. diaphragmatic hernia).  The segment has its own pleura and therefore collateral air drift via the pores of Kohn cannot occur. The lack of aeration helps differentiate it from intralobar sequestration. Seen on a CXR as an opacity adjacent to the heart, abutting the diaphragm.

Thymoma

As a differential diagnosis of a thoracic low attenuation lesion, thymomas can be included. They are usually anterosuperior in location however, although may, if sufficiently large, extend as far down as the diaphragm. Although they can be surrounded by fat any low attenuation seen within the mass is actually due to necrosis  and fibrosis rather than fat within the mass. They can also contain calcification in amorphous or curvilinear formations. Features of invasion which would point towards a malignant thymoma as opposed to a benign one would include an irregular outline, spread along the pleura and invasion of the mediastinal fat.

Cardiac fat pad

There is fat around the heart in everyone but in some individuals, and in those of a higher BMI, this can be more prominent. The right side usually has more prominent fat pads than the left but both can be seen on CXRs if sufficiently prominent.

stem: A 6-week-old baby boy is referred to his local paediatric services after the health visitor raised concerns that his skin hip creases were asymmetrical. Following review by a paediatric consultant a diagnosis of developmental dysplasia of the hip is suspected. He is referred for an ultrasound scan.
prompt: Regarding the alpha angle, which of the following is correct?
options: Between the bony ilium and the cartilaginous roof
In the normal patient it should be >60o
It cannot be measured on ultrasound
It is determined using Hilgenreiner and Perkin's lines
It is used to determine the subtype of dyplasia present
explanation:
Developmental dysplasia of the hip

This condition is screened for clinically at birth using the Ortolani and Barlow tests where the hips are flexed and externally rotated according to specific movements. Unfortunately, some cases are not picked up this way and are discovered later around the time the child would usually be expected to begin weight bearing and walking. Asymmetric hip skin creases also provide another diagnostic clue although this finding is prone to overdiagnosis.

In babies younger than four months ultrasound is the first modality of choice as the femoral head is not yet ossified. Ultrasound is performed with the hip flexed and the probe placed perpendicular on the lateral aspect of the hip and to the orientation of the femur. Alpha and beta angles are measured to determine whether the femoral head is correctly located within the acetabulum. The alpha angle is the angle between the roof of the acetabulum and the vertical aspect of the ilium. The normal alpha angle measures >60o. The beta angle is far more variable and is more useful for determining the subtype of hip dysplasia.

Beyond around 4 months of age, the femoral head becomes ossified and difficult to image on ultrasound. An AP radiograph becomes the optimum method of diagnosis.

Three different eponymous lines are used to determine whether the hip is dysplastic. In the normal patient the femoral head should lie in the lower, inner quadrant created by the intersection of Perkin and Hilgenreiners lines:

Hilgenreiner's line (aide memoire - H for horizontal) - this line extends between the triradiate cartilages on either side

Perkin's line (aide memoire - P for perpendicular) - this line is drawn perpendicular to Hilgenreiner's line at the superolateral point of the acetabulum.

Shenton's line - this is a curved line drawn along the lower border of the superior pubic ramus and extending across the joint to the medial border of the proximal femoral shaft. The same line is useful in adults to try to identify femoral neck fractures. Discontinuity to the line suggests possible DDH.

The acetabular angle is the radiological equivalent of the alpha angle in ultrasound. It is drawn from the superior aspect of the acetabulum to intersect with Hilgenreiner's line. Normal is <30o if under 12 months old and <24o thereafter.

stem: An athletic 14-year-old boy is taken to A+E by his mum after developing a painful right hip. An x-ray demonstrates an irregular shaped bone adjacent to the ischial tuberosity.
prompt: The avulsion of which muscle is most likely to have caused this injury?
explanation:
Apophyseal injuries (avulsion fractures) are common in adolescents because the tendons are stronger than the secondary ossification centres. By definition they occur in the unfused skeleton.

Other avulsion fractures do occur in children and adults alike but those in the table all take place at secondary ossification centres around the pelvis.

Of note, in an adult the avulsion of the lesser trochanter suggests a metastasis, not a musculoskeletal injury.

stem: A 7-year-old girl undergoes a renal tract ultrasound for recurrent urinary tract infections. This demonstrates both kidneys lying centrally in the abdomen, connected by a band of renal tissue.
prompt: What normal structure limits the superior migration of a horseshoe kidney?
explanation:
A horseshoe kidney is the most common renal fusion abnormality. It’s associated with multiple complications including susceptibility to trauma, stones, infection and tumours. There is also an associated with Turner syndrome. The IMA prevents further superior migration of the fused kidneys.

Crossed fused ectopia is the next most common renal fusion abnormality. Similar complications are present although there is no increased risk of tumour development.

Eagle Barrett syndrome (prune belly) is a complex malformation with absence of the rectus abdominis, bilateral severe hydroureter/ hydronephrosis, cryptorchidism.

stem: A 5-year-old who has had a runny nose for two weeks presents via A+E with drowsiness and a reduced level of consciousness. An MRI of his head shows bilateral multifocal and confluent areas of high signal on T2 and FLAIR.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis

This is an autoimmune, post-viral demyelinating entity usually affecting young adults or children. MRI findings of bilateral asymmetrical areas of T2/FLAIR hyperintensities are classical. These can be confluent or punctuate. There is an excellent and dramatic response to steroids.

Hurst disease

This is a fulminant haemorrhagic version of ADEM.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)

This is a JC virus mediated phenomenon which causes asymmetrical patchy white matter changes. These can be bilateral. The testable feature is involvement of the cortical U-fibres which separates it from HIV encephalopathy where the U-fibres are spared.

Guillain-Barre syndrome

Guillain-Barre syndrome which is an autoimmune mediated ascending flaccid paralysis. Most imaging will be normal in such cases, with the exception of some possible contrast enhancement and thickening to the nerve roots at the cauda equina.

Multiple sclerosis

This is an idiopathic demyelinating disease with oedematous perivascular inflammation in the acute stage progressing to demyelination with proliferation of the astroglia in the chronic phase. There are oblong elliptical plaques of high T2 signal at the callososeptal interface.

Other highly testable features:

Involvement of the middle cerebellar peduncle is specific to multiple sclerosis when attempting to differentiate it from small vessel ischaemic changes

Lesions can cross the midline

Axial T2 sequences are better than FLAIR for posterior fossa lesions

Acute lesions can enhance with contrast, classically in an ‘incomplete ring’

Thalamic involvement is rare and suggests the possibility of ADEM instead

stem: You are reviewing the chest radiograph of a baby boy. He is being followed up for a known cyanotic congenital heart anomaly.
prompt: Which of the following diagnoses is he most likely to have?
explanation:
None of the answers above would usually be considered as typical cyanotic congenital heart disease however, hypoplastic left heart syndrome can cause cyanosis.

Hypoplastic left heart syndrome

This condition is duct dependant; the underdeveloped left heart is insufficient to deliver blood to the body. A right-to-left shunt must exist such that the right sided pressures can be transmitted to the descending thoracic aorta. Similarly, a left-to-right shunt through a patent foramen ovale also exists to deliver the oxygenated blood from the lungs to the right side of the heart. This causes significant mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood which can be sufficient to cause clinical cyanosis. Patients present in the neonatal period (if not antenatally diagnosed) with severe cardiogenic shock following the closure of the ductus arteriosus at around day 4-5 of life.
