On imaging the masses are usually heterogenous. Cystic areas can often be seen secondary to areas of necrosis. The claw sign occurs when there is a rim of normal renal tissue extending part of the way around the mass. A Wilms tumour is often described as enhancing but less so than the adjacent normal renal parenchyma.

stem: A 6-week-old girl is referred to the hospital by the health visitor for failure to progress. She undergoes an x-ray which shows cardiomegaly and a large mass in the right upper quadrant. An ultrasound scan reveals a complex poorly-defined 10cm mass in the right lobe of the liver which contains multiple vascular channels.
prompt: Which additional feature would make you consider a haemangioendothelioma the most likely diagnosis? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Haemangioendothelioma

These are benign lesions which can cause elevation of the serum AFP and endothelial growth factor but the vast majority occur in babies under the age of 6 months. Around half of cases are associated with the presence of a cutaneous haemangioma. They are large vascular tumours and on imaging behave as might be expected of a haemangioma with low echogenicity on ultrasound, peripheral enhancement with gradual filling in on CT and flow voids on MRI. Calcifications can be seen with these lesions but they are finer, more granular calcifications; not coarse. Owing to their size they often cause significant right to left shunting of blood resulting in congestive heart failure. Thrombocytopaenia also occurs due to platelet trapping (known as the Kasabach-Merritt sequence). N.B. these lesions should not be confused with epithelioid haemangioendotheliomas which occur in adults.

Hepatic masses in children © Medical Exam Prep

stem: A 15-year-old boy suffers a knee injury while on a skiing holiday. He visits a local hospital and has x-rays taken of his knee. No fracture is found. Once back home he undergoes an MRI scan when the pain fails to resolve. He is told he has a pivot shift type injury.
prompt: What findings on MRI would be most consistent with this?
options: High STIR signal to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated posterior cruciate ligament tear
High T2 signal to the anterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau with an anterior cruciate ligament and medial collateral ligament tear
High signal on STIR to the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau with an associated tear of the anterior cruciate ligament tear
High signal on T2 and STIR to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated anterior cruciate ligament tear
High signal on T2 to the lateral femoral condyle and medial patella facet with an associated tear of the medial retinaculum
explanation:
Bony contusions

Bruising to the bone can be detected around 2 days following an injury but may not resolve for many months thereafter. With regards knee injuries, it is often possible to discern the mechanism of injury from the pattern of bruising seen. The contusions follow fluid on MRI scans i.e. low in signal on T1 and high on T2 (and STIR). STIR is used to suppress the fat of the bone marrow thereby making the fluid stand out more.

Clip injury and pivot shift injury

- High signal on STIR to the lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau with an associated tear of the anterior cruciate ligament tear (Pivot shift)

- High T2 signal to the anterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau with an anterior cruciate ligament and medial collateral ligament tear (Clip injury)

These two injuries are very similar. Both involve valgus stress on a flexed knee (such as a tackle to the knee during sports). A pivot shift injury also requires external rotation of the tibia. The three main structures most at risk during these injuries are:

Anterior cruciate ligament (especially in a pivot shift injury)

Medial collateral ligament (especially in a clip injury)

Medial meniscus (remember that the medial meniscus is attached to the medial collateral ligament)

If all three are present together it is referred to as the O’Donoghue triad. Since O’Donoghue defined this triad however, it has been discovered that lateral meniscal tears are actually more common with this type of injury than medial meniscus ones.

Bony contusions occur at the side of impact because the proximal tibia and distal femur impact on one another thus:

Lateral tibial plateau (posterolateral in pivot shift injury)

Lateral femoral condyle

Transient lateral patella dislocation injury - High signal on T2 to the lateral femoral condyle and medial patella facet with an associated tear of the medial retinaculum

When the patella dislocates laterally, its medial facet can impact onto the anterolateral corner of the lateral femoral condyle. Both areas become damaged and contusions can be seen on MRI. Often though, the patella reduces spontaneously and thus the exact mechanism of injury must be inferred from the imaging findings.

Joint effusion

Osteochondral injuries to the anterolateral femoral condyle and medial patella facet

Sprain or disruption to the medial retinaculum

Hyperextension injury - High signal on T2 and STIR to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated anterior cruciate ligament tear

These occur often following excessively forceful kicking. There will be bony contusions at the anterior aspect of the tibial plateau and femoral condyles. Either of the anterior or posterior cruciate ligaments may also be involved.

Dashboard injury - High STIR signal to the anterior aspect of the tibia with an associated posterior cruciate ligament tear

As the name would suggest, this injury is usually stained by impact of the knee against the dashboard of a car during a road traffic incident. Force applied to the anterior aspect of the tibia when the knee is flexed leads to:

Osteochondral injury or fracture to the anterior aspect of the tibia

Posterior cruciate ligament rupture/sprain

stem: A baby boy attends his GP surgery for routine immunisations at 12 weeks old. The practice nurse is concerned that the baby's head is an unusual shape and asks the GP to see the baby. She agrees and the baby is referred to the paediatric services at your local hospital. A CT is performed which shows premature fusion of a cranial suture.
prompt: Which suture is most commonly involved in craniosynostosis?
explanation:
Craniosynostosis

Premature closure of one or more of the sutures leads to an abnormal shape to the head developing as the brain continues to grow within a confined space.

Of these by far the most common is sagittal craniosynostosis which causes elongation of the skull and is termed scaphocephaly meaning 'boat-like'.

stem: You are reviewing the chest radiograph of a baby boy. He is being followed up for a known cyanotic congenital heart anomaly.
prompt: Which of the following diagnoses is he LEAST likely to have?
explanation:
Please note that the question asks which is the LEAST likely diagnosis.

Image © Medical Exam Prep

Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)

TOF (not to be confused with trache-oesophageal fistula) causes cyanosis but without pulmonary plethora thus is not included in the 5 Ts.

The tetrat consists of:

VSD

Overriding aorta

Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)

RV outflow obstruction (hence pulmonary oligaemia)

TOF is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease presenting after 12 months of age. In ambulant children the classic finding is of squatting whereby the child squats following exertion in order to increase blood flow to the lungs. It usually presents by at least 3-4 months of age however, but at birth the condition can be concealed by shunting of blood through a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). Another facet to the clinical presentation can be polycythaemia which takes place due to chronic low oxygen levels.

Owing to the RVH the cardiac apex is turned upwards contributing to an appearance referred to as ‘boot shaped’ to the cardiac shadow on a CXR.

There is a strong association with right sided aortic arch. Nearly all right sided arches are associated with some form of congenital heart disease and most of these are TOF. Conversely 25% of TOF patients also have a right sided aortic arch.

Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR)

Anomalous pulmonary venous return can be partial or total. In the latter, the oxygenated blood returning from the lungs fails to drain into the left side of the heart but reaches the right side of the heart by other avenues. Such babies are dependent on a right-to-left shunt (usually an ASD). TAPVR is not a duct-dependant condition (which usually present around day 4-5 when the duct closes) but can also present in the very early neonatal period with unstable cyanosis.

Most patients with this condition return the oxygenated blood from the lungs to the right side of the heart via either the brachiocephalic veins or the coronary sinus. Excessive pressures on the lungs cause pulmonary plethora and, if not picked up antenatally or neonatally, can compensate for the initial few weeks and months. Owing to the prominence of the supracardiac vasculature, the appearance on a chest radiograph is said to resemble a snowman.

Transposition of the Great Vessels (TGA)

When the great vessels are transposed there exists two independent circulations. This is therefore only compatible with life if a shunt mechanism also exists, such as an ASD, VSD or PDA. The CXR can be initially normal but develops an ‘egg on side’ appearance to the cardiac shadow. In some cases the transposition is ‘corrected’  where the ventricles are also switched such that the correct ventricle feeds the correct great vessel although the left and right sided circulations remain separate. In corrected transposition the CXR features of note are an apparently absent pulmonary trunk, and an abnormal aortic contour.

stem: An 11-week-old baby boy is referred to his local paediatric services after the health visitor noticed that his hip skin creases were asymmetric. Following review by a paediatric consultant a diagnosis of developmental dysplasia of the hip is suspected.
prompt: How should this best be investigated?
explanation:
Developmental dysplasia of the hip

This condition is screened for clinically at birth using the Ortolani and Barlow tests where the hips are flexed and externally rotated according to specific movements. Unfortunately, some cases are not picked up this way and are discovered later around the time the child would usually be expected to begin weight bearing and walking. Asymmetric hip skin creases also provide another diagnostic clue although this finding is prone to overdiagnosis.

In babies younger than four months ultrasound is the first modality of choice as the femoral head is not yet ossified. Ultrasound is performed with the hip flexed and the probe placed perpendicular on the lateral aspect of the hip and to the orientation of the femur. Alpha and beta angles are measured to determine whether the femoral head is correctly located within the acetabulum. The alpha angle is the angle between the roof of the acetabulum and the vertical aspect of the ilium. The normal alpha angle measures >60o. The beta angle is far more variable and is more useful for determining the subtype of hip dysplasia.

Beyond around 4 months of age, the femoral head becomes ossified and difficult to image on ultrasound. An AP radiograph becomes the optimum method of diagnosis.

Three different eponymous lines are used to determine whether the hip is dysplastic. In the normal patient the femoral head should lie in the lower, inner quadrant created by the intersection of Perkin and Hilgenreiners lines:

Hilgenreiner's line (aide memoire - H for horizontal) - this line extends between the triradiate cartilages on either side

Perkin's line (aide memoire - P for perpendicular) - this line is drawn perpendicular to Hilgenreiner's line at the superolateral point of the acetabulum.

Shenton's line - this is a curved line drawn along the lower border of the superior pubic ramus and extending across the joint to the medial border of the proximal femoral shaft. The same line is useful in adults to try to identify femoral neck fractures. Discontinuity to the line suggests possible DDH.

The acetabular angle is the radiological equivalent of the alpha angle in ultrasound. It is drawn from the superior aspect of the acetabulum to intersect with Hilgenreiner's line. Normal is <30o if under 12 months old and <24o thereafter.

stem: A 9-year-old girl presents with pain and tenderness to the forearm after falling over in the playground at school. She undergoes radiographs of her arm and a fracture to the shaft of the ulna with angulation at the fracture site is readily appreciable.
prompt: What is the most likely associated injury?
options: Anterior dislocation of the radial head
Associated radial shaft fracture and anterior dislocation of the radial head
Dislocation at the distal radio-ulnar joint
explanation:
A Monteggia fracture-dislocation typically occurs following a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH) and consists of an ulnar fracture with a radial head dislocation.

Dislocation at the distal radio-ulnar joint in association with a radial fracture is termed Galeazzi fracture and results from a FOOSH injury where the elbow is flexed at the point of impact.

stem: A 1-year-old girl is brought to the Emergency Department by her parents. She has severe abdominal tenderness and distension. Ultrasound demonstrates an ileocolic intussusception. She is brought round to the radiology department for an attempt at reduction by fluoroscopically guided air enema. Your assistant suggests you remove the grid before beginning the procedure.
prompt: Which of the following regarding grids is correct? Select ONE answer only.
options: Grids are not necessary for paediatric patients
Grids help reduce the effect of patient motion
Use of a grid increases the dose to the patient
Use of a grid significantly increases dose to the operator
Without the grid there is no need to wear lead aprons
explanation:
Grids

An anti-scatter grid is useful for patients heavier than around 20kg (about age 4-5) when scatter from within the patient reduces the image quality but, especially for patients smaller than this, the grid only serves to increase the patient dose (by only allowing direct photons through, a greater number of photons must be supplied to create the resultant image). Without any numbers or calculations to perform it is difficult to compare the effects of grid removal and field of view however in this patient the grid should definitely not be used as the patient is too small.

Magnification and FOV

Image magnification can be achieved either via geometric or electronic means. Geometric magnification reduces patient dose by moving the patient further away from the radiation source however the further the patient is from the source, the greater the blurring effect of any patient (or bowel, or respiratory) motion. Electronic magnification is also called changing the field of view (think of this like zooming) and increasing the FOV does reduce the dose, but at the expense of image sharpness. The dose saving can be significant owing to the inverse square law.

Collimation

Collimating the x-ray beam involves using lead shielding to concentrate the x-ray beam onto the target area (think of this like cropping). It is important to avoid irradiating tissue which is not required for diagnosis but also reduces operator dose by reducing scatter from the irradiated patient. This may be challenging in a paediatric intussusception scan as it relies on the patient lying still within the target area.

Continuous vs pulsed

Continuous fluoroscopy mode (as opposed to pulsed fluoroscopy) involves, as the name suggests, imaging continuously as opposed to taking an image at pulsed intervals which involves far less dose. Moving objects are also better imaged with pulsed mode as there can be significant blurring when using continuous fluoroscopy.

stem: A 15-year-old boy is studying for some science exams. While attempting to recall the bones in the arm he notices a subcutaneous fusiform mass on his forearm which is not present in the diagram in his book. His GP refers him for an ultrasound scan which shows the mass to bear a similar echogenicity to muscle.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
There are many different minor accessory muscle possibilities at the wrist/forearm. The mass described has a similar reflectivity to muscle.

Muscular hernia

Muscular hernias are more often seen in the lower limbs than the upper limbs. They can be diagnosed with ultrasound when a lump of muscle can be seen protruding through a defect in the containing fascia. Clinically a patient with a lump which disappears when the underlying muscle is tensed should raise the suspicion of a muscular hernia.

Ganglion cyst

These are fluid-filled masses associated with musculoskeletal structures. They are most recognisable in the wrist. Due to pressure effects on locally adjacent nerves they can be associated with numbness. On imaging they behave as would be expected for cystic masses however owing to a variable protein content of the gelatinous content they can return high signal on T1 weighted MRI sequences.

Giant Cell Tumour also known as osteoclastoma

These are benign bony tumours arising from within bone. They can cause bony expansion from within but not bony scalloping from without. Since they always occur in the mature skeleton they are seldom found in children or adolescent patients although the peak age group is still young; 30s. Typically they occur around the knee but can be found anywhere in the skeleton. They are seen on x-ray as expansile lytic lesions with the words ‘soap bubble’ often used to describe them in literature. On MRI they usually return low signal on both T1 and T2, in contrast to many of the potential differential diagnoses which would otherwise return high signal on one or the other.

Four criteria of GCT (according to Clyde A. Helms)

After epiphyseal closure

Abuts articular surface

Well defined, non-sclerotic margin

Eccentric location

Rhabdomyosarcoma

These are often aggressive lesions which can be found anywhere in the body. Although histologically they are formed of skeletal muscle derivation, they do not have to be in continuity with normal skeletal muscle. They tend to appear low in reflectivity on ultrasound. On MRI they follow muscle on T1 weighted sequences, but enhance avidly with gadolinium.

stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to A+E following a fall from a trampoline. He is refusing to weight bear through his left leg and an x-ray reveals a fracture. The fracture line runs through the lateral aspect of the epiphyseal plate and the centre of the epiphysis.
prompt: What is the Salter-Harris classification of this fracture?
explanation:
Salter-Harris classification

The Salter-Harris classification is used to stratify fractures of the unfused skeleton according to their risk of developing deformity.

stem: A 13-year-old boy has a chest radiograph to investigate a history of chest pain. A wedge of hazy opacification is seen in the lung. In addition, there are coarse bony trabeculations and an H-shaped vertebrae at the level of T7. Furthermore, a posterior mediastinal mass extending over multiple vertebral levels is identified.
prompt: What is the most likely aetiology of the posterior mediastinal mass?
explanation:
The differential diagnosis of a posterior mediastinal mass is an important one to know. The key features in this question are the lung infarct and H-shaped vertebra which indicate an underlying diagnosis of sickle cell disease.

Extramedullary haematompoesis

Coarse bone trabeculations and an adjacent posterior mediastinal mass are key to the diagnosis. Extramedullary hematopoiesis can be found in multiple organ systems, but most commonly the liver, spleen and lymph nodes. Lesions are FDG avid on a PET-CTscan.

Neuroenteric cyst

This would be a cystic lesion and is often associated with spinal anomalies (E.g. hemivertebrae) and therefore scoliosis.

Neurofibroma & Ganglioneuromas

This would be a round mass in the posterior mediastinum usually in a child above the age of 10.

Neuroblastoma

For a posterior mediastinal mass in a child under the age of 10, a neuroblastoma should be the top differential diagnosis to be considered. Usually it is heterogeneous with calcification and areas of necrosis.

stem: A 16-year-old, on holiday with some friends, and known to have cystic fibrosis, is taken to A+E by her friends after developing severe abdominal pain over the last two days. While waiting to be seen in A+E she also begins vomiting. An abdominal radiograph shows a bubbly area in the right lower quadrant.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Distal Intestinal Obstruction Syndrome (DIOS)

The description of a bubbly area on an abdominal radiograph is more usually linked to meconium ileus. DIOS is also referred to as a meconium ileus equivalent as these two conditions are similar. In patients with cystic fibrosis the thicker-than-normal intestinal mucus, increase in transit time and pancreatic insufficiency all conspire to cause faecal impaction. This often occurs in early adolescence when parental control wears thin and concordance with medical management (in particular pancreatic enzyme replacement) of their cystic fibrosis can become an issue. Patients develop colicky right lower quadrant pain and tenderness when faecal matter obstructs around the terminal ileum. On x-ray this can sometimes be seen as a bubbly area close to where the caecum might be expected to be.

Fibrosing colonopathy

By contrast this condition is caused by pancreatic enzyme replacement. High dose lipase treatment leads to progressive stricturing of the colonic submucosa. Modern preparations of enzyme supplementation have reduced the incidence of this disease.

stem: An 11-year-old boy has a mass in his right cerebellopontine angle. CT shows a lobulated homogeneous mass with CSF density. MRI shows low T1 signal and high T2 signal. There is restriction on diffusion weighted imaging and hyperintensity on FLAIR sequences.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
There are a few key features to cerebellopontine angle masses which help distinguish them from one another. In this particular question the combination of CSF density on CT with hyperintensity on FLAIR gives the game away. This is classic for an epidermoid cyst. Additionally, restricted diffusion is specific for an epidermoid cyst. A choroid plexus cyst is not a CP angle mass.

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the Emergency Department by his parents. They report that he fell over the back of their sofa and hit his head. He is examined and x-rays are taken.
prompt: Which of the following is most suggestive of a non-accidental injury? Select ONE answer only.
explanation:
Spiral fractures can be caused by both accidental and non-accidental injuries but are more common in adults than children. Significant power is needed to cause a spiral fracture in a child; they are unusual in the setting of a straightforward fall.

Non-accidental injury

It is the responsibility of all members of the healthcare profession to be alert to the possibility of non-accidental injury. For radiologists, there are specific findings which should alert the reporter to the possibility of non-accidental injury. These include:

Lower limb injuries in a non-ambulant child

Discrepancy between the history and apparent injuries

Delay seeking medical attention

Metaphyseal fractures (corner or bucket-handle)

Multiple fractures of different ages

Scapula fractures

Posterior rib fractures

Sternal fractures

Skull fractures (especially non-parietal, or crossing sutures)

It is important to appreciate that any fracture (not just the ones listed above) can be caused by non-accidental injury.

A skeletal survey to investigate for the presence of further fractures includes:

Two views of the skull (frontal and lateral)

AP of upper limbs (over multiple films if necessary)

DP of wrist/hand

Lateral of elbow and wrist

AP of lower limbs (over multiple films if necessary)

DP feet

AP ankle

Lateral of ankle and knee

AP abdomen and pelvis

Three views of the chest (frontal and two oblique)

Lateral whole spine

CT head - if younger than 1 year, or older than 1 year with head trauma or abnormal neurology, or older than 2

Siblings younger than age 2 should also have the same imaging as the index patient.

stem: On the ward round of the neonatal intensive care unit, a baby is reviewed. She was born a week ago at 33+4 weeks gestation. She has been receiving mechanical ventilation but her oxygen saturations have deteriorated during the last 24 hours.  A chest x-ray shows slight overinflation with black streaks radiating from the hilum.
prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Of the five main respiratory conditions of the neonate the differential diagnosis can be narrowed based on gestational age.  The presence of hyperinflation can also be useful but may not always be present where feasible so should not be used as an absolute discriminator. If present, it is useful.

Meconium aspiration

Meconium is sticky and causes a chemical pneumonitis in the lungs, seen as patchy consolidation. In addition small globules of meconium entering bronchi and bronchioles of a decreasing calibre act as a ball-valve mechanism and lead to air trapping; thus the lung volumes of a baby with meconium aspiration may be increased. Air bronchograms are notably absent. The typical baby in a meconium aspiration situation is post-term.

Transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN)

The classical patient for TTN would be a term baby born by caesarean section to a diabetic mother. During normal vaginal delivery the compression of the baby as it descends the birth canal acts to squeeze fluid out from its lungs. This mechanism is all but absent during a caesarean section.  Consequently these babies are born with an excess of retained fluid. The CXR of an affected baby will show bilateral symmetrical air space opacification with air bronchograms, fluid in the fissures and pleural effusions. This peaks in severity at 24hrs but resolves by three days.

Hyaline Membrane Disease (HMD) also known as surfactant deficient disease (SDD)

It is to reduce the likelihood of this disease developing that a woman in pre-term labour will be offered a steroid injection. The steroids help the neonatal lungs to develop faster and increase the likelihood of their being able to produce surfactant once delivered. Where there is surfactant deficiency the alveoli collapse. The CXR will show a granular opacification throughout both lungs which progresses to bilateral ground glass opacification with air bronchograms. If exogenous surfactant is given to the baby there may be asymmetrical improvement in the appearances depending on how much reaches each lung. Of note HMD does not cause pleural effusions. Finally a normal CXR at 6hrs post delivery excludes HMD.

Pulmonary interstitial emphysema (PIE)

As the name would suggest, this disease is diagnosed when there is air within the interstitial tissues of the lungs. It is caused by alveolar rupture due to the barotrauma of mechanical ventilation or positive airway pressure.  It can be associated with hyaline membrane disease and is prevalent in infants of a low birth weight. Complications such as pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum can be severe and acutely life threatening. Radiographically there is hyperinflation and lucencies in either a cystic pattern or streaks emanating from the hila and following the direction of the bronchi/bronchioles. It is treated with high frequency oscillation ventilation which is less traumatic to the lungs.

Bronchopulmonary dysplasia

This also occurs due to barotrauma in ventilated neonates but is a more gradual process, occurring later on in the baby’s life; perhaps after a couple of weeks. Typically (but not exclusively) the baby is premature (hence requiring ventilation). It only usually occurs after the baby in question has received ventilation of >21% oxygen for longer than 28 days. The lungs are hyperinflated and what starts off as ground glass opacification becomes complete opacification with air bronchograms in a few days. After 30 days it can be seen as coarse linear lucencies, described as radiating from the hila, with focal emphysematous change. Mikity syndrome has similar features and includes early develompent of interstitisal emphysema. It occurs in premature babies but is rarely seen now due to significant improvements in ventilation equipment.

stem: You are reviewing a CXR of a patient who has an elevated left hemidiaphragm.
prompt: Which of the following pieces of information would be most useful in explaining it?
explanation:
This question examines the differential diagnosis of an elevated hemidaphragm.

Diaphragmatic palsy can be caused by an infarction involving the contralateral internal capsule. This is usually supplied by the middle cerebral artery.

Scoliosis of the spine can take many appearances and the exact effect on the thorax differs from patient to patient.

Splenectomy if anything would cause depression of the diaphragm but usually has no perceptible effect on it.

A previous RTA would only impact on the diaphragm were there to be a diaphragmatic rupture.

Supradiaphragmatic

Diaphragmatic

Infradiaphragmatic
